# A ```{typst} block looks like an executable cell to Quarto's engine
# detection, which then selects Jupyter and fails for want of a kernel. The
# extension compiles those blocks itself, so the page needs no engine.
engine: markdown
---

`typst_define()` pushes named values from a knitr or Jupyter session into the `{typst}` blocks of the document.
Each value is read back as `#typst_define.<name>`.

::: {.callout-note}
This page shows the source only.
These documentation pages carry no R or Python session, so the figure at the end draws the same values written as literals.
:::

## Setup

Two helpers ship with the extension, under `_extensions/mcanouil/typst-render/_resources/`.
There is no Julia helper, so this covers knitr and Jupyter alone.

The R helper needs `rlang` and `jsonlite`:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| include: false
source("_extensions/mcanouil/typst-render/_resources/typst_define.R")
```
````

The Python helper needs `IPython`:

````markdown
```{{python}}
#| include: false
import sys
sys.path.insert(0, "_extensions/mcanouil/typst-render/_resources")
from typst_define import typst_define
```
````

The R helper also registers a passthrough engine for `typst` blocks, which knitr needs.
A document that uses knitr without the helper registers it itself:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| include: false
knitr::knit_engines$set(typst = function(options) {
  knitr::asis_output(paste0("\n```{typst}\n", paste(options[["code"]], collapse = "\n"), "\n```\n"))
})
```
````

Without that registration knitr claims the cell, knows no `typst` engine, and writes the source to the page with no figure beside it.
See [Engines](../reference.qmd#engines).

## Defining values

Call the helper wherever the values are ready:

````markdown
```{{r}}
#| include: false
typst_define(
  title = "Fuel economy",
  d = data.frame(cyl = c(4L, 6L, 8L), mpg = c(26.7, 19.7, 15.1))
)
```
````

The call emits a hidden metadata block, so it adds nothing to the page.

## Reading them in a block

A scalar is read by name, and a data frame column is an array:

````markdown
```{typst}
#typst_define.title, first column value #typst_define.d.mpg.at(0)
```
````

A figure draws the column:

````markdown
```{typst}
#stack(
  dir: ltr,
  spacing: 6pt,
  ..typst_define.d.mpg.map(value => rect(width: 1cm, height: value * 1.2pt, fill: teal.lighten(40%))),
)
```
````

The same figure, with the column written as a literal so this page can compile it:

```{typst}
//| echo: false
#stack(
  dir: ltr,
  spacing: 6pt,
  ..(26.7, 19.7, 15.1).map(value => rect(width: 1cm, height: value * 1.2pt, fill: teal.lighten(40%))),
)
```

Every `{typst}` block of the document reads the same values, wherever it sits.
The engine runs the whole document before the filter does, so a block above the call sees them as well.

## What each type becomes

| From R or Python | In Typst |
| --- | --- |
| Scalar, string, boolean | The same value. |
| Array, nested object | A Typst array, a Typst dictionary. |
| R data frame, pandas or polars data frame | A dictionary of arrays, one per column. |
| numpy array | A Typst array. |
| `NULL`, `NA`, `None` | Typst `none`. |

: How a defined value arrives in a block. {.striped .hover tbl-colwidths="[52,48]"}

Read a column by name and never by position, because the keys of a carried object arrive sorted by name.
The [Reference](../reference.qmd#passing-data-from-r-or-python) gives the remaining rules: the order of the names, the `_row` key of an R data frame, and what a repeated name does.
